prompt: Describe, in terms of electron transfer, how an ionic bond forms between a potassium atom (K, 1 valence electron) and sulfur atoms (S, 6 valence electrons each), and name the ions that result. Then predict whether solid K₂S conducts electricity, and whether molten K₂S conducts, explaining BOTH predictions in terms of the structure you have described.
answer:
Each potassium atom loses its 1 valence electron to reach the stable configuration of the noble gas before it, forming a K⁺ ion. Each sulfur atom gains 2 electrons to complete its outer shell, forming a sulfide ion, S²⁻. The charges must cancel, so the compound contains two potassium ions for every sulfide ion, giving the formula K₂S. The oppositely charged ions attract one another in every direction and build a rigid lattice.

Solid K₂S does NOT conduct. The ions are charged, but each one is locked in place in the lattice, and a current needs charge that can MOVE. Molten K₂S DOES conduct: melting supplies enough energy to break the lattice apart, the K⁺ and S²⁻ ions become free to move, and they carry charge through the liquid.
explanation: The prediction is the part that cannot be recited, and it turns on a distinction learners often miss: having charged particles is not the same as being able to conduct. An ionic solid is made entirely of ions and still insulates, because conduction needs those charges to be mobile. Melting does not change what the particles are — it changes only whether they can move — which is why the same substance switches from insulator to conductor with no chemical change at all. Dissolving it in water does the same thing for the same reason. A metal is the contrast worth holding alongside this: it conducts as a solid, because there the mobile charges are delocalised electrons rather than whole ions.
